newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Avonmore, Waterford fate in balance.
newsitem.headline: Avonmore, Waterford fate in balance.

text.p: The fate of Ireland's dairy industry will be decided later today as shareholders meet to vote on a proposed merger between Ireland's two largest food companies on Friday.

The meeting, deemed the most important meeting in the history of the Irish farmers co-operative movement, began at 1200 local time (1100 GMT) simultaneously in Ireland's midland town of Kilkenny and southern county of Waterford.
Avonmore Foods, Ireland's biggest single dairy company, launched a 281 million Irish pound ($427.9 million) merger offer for rival Waterford Foods in early April.
This was rejected by Waterford, which claimed the bid undervalued the company.
A revised offer of 337 million Irish pounds, announced in May, got the go-ahead from the Waterford board and will be voted on today by both co-ops members.

Avonmore shareholders, meeting in Kilkenny, are expected to vote yes to the merger, but the outcome of the Waterford co-op vote hangs in the balance as farmers fear massive job cuts resulting from the highly synergistic merger.
A second round of meetings will be held on July 25 to ratify a thumbs-up to the merger. A 'no vote' by either co-op will end all merger talks.
If approved, the merger will weld together two of Ireland's premier food companies with a joint turnover of 2.5 billion Irish pounds and pre-tax profits of 71.5 million.
This would create the largest dairy company in Britain and Ireland and the fourth largest milk processor in the world.

Analysts said the merged company's milk production would far outstrip the dairy operations of Britain's Northern Foods Plc and Unigate Plc and its cheese production would account for 20 percent of the British market.
The chairmen of Avonmore Foods AVFa.L and Waterford Foods Plc urged members of the two Co-operatives on July 1 to back merger proposals.
John Dowley, Waterford's chairman, and John Duggan, his counterpart at Avonmore, said the merger would create a farmer-controlled organisation capable of competing in local and international markets.
They said this was essential to ensure above average returns to its farmers into the next century.
A 75 percent majority of those present and voting at each meeting is required to approve the merger.
It is the second time in six years that Avonmore has attempted to merge with Waterford after a similar attempt in 1991 failed.
The two companies have interests in Europe, Britain and America. Avonmore has interests in meat products, animal foodstuffs and agricultural products including grain.
It has processing operations in Ireland, Britain, Belgium and the United States, Japan, Korea and Singapore.
Waterford is engaged in dairy-based food products, fruit juices and animal foodstuffs and has processing plants in Ireland, Britain and America.
